Atelectasis on chest radiographs: 5

A patient with fever has a lobar opacity containing air bronchograms, but the fissures and diaphragm retain their positions and there is no appreciable volume loss. Which process better fits this description than assuming every opacity is atelectasis?

  1. Pulmonary volume loss
  2. Shift toward the side of volume loss
  3. Displacement of a fissure toward the collapsed lobe
  4. Resorption atelectasis from airway obstruction
  5. Air-space consolidation without appreciable volume loss
Answer and explanation

Air-space consolidation without appreciable volume loss

Alveolar filling can produce opacity and air bronchograms while preserving volume; opacity alone does not establish collapse.

Option explanations

Air-space consolidation without appreciable volume loss: Alveolar filling can produce opacity and air bronchograms while preserving volume; opacity alone does not establish collapse.

Pulmonary volume loss: Atelectasis combines reduced aeration with loss of lung volume, helping distinguish it from uncomplicated air-space filling. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Shift toward the side of volume loss: Substantial collapse can pull the mediastinum toward the affected side; a pressure-producing pleural process may push it away. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Displacement of a fissure toward the collapsed lobe: Fissural movement is a useful local sign of lobar volume loss. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Resorption atelectasis from airway obstruction: A blocked bronchus prevents replenishment of alveolar gas, which is absorbed, allowing distal collapse. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
